title: Quasiparticle interference: momentum structure and phase limits
summary: Read Fourier-transform tunneling maps with their scattering, sampling and phase assumptions. Distinguish measured modulation from inferred bands, gap sign and competing order.

claims.statement: Quasiparticle interference (QPI) uses spatial variations in scanning tunneling conductance to constrain electronic states and scattering. Elastic scattering can connect states of equal energy with momentum transfer $\mathbf q=\mathbf k'-\mathbf k$. A Fourier peak is a feature of a measured response, not a direct photograph of a Fermi surface or a uniquely identified order parameter. Keep the tunneling matrix element, defect channel and preprocessing attached to every interpretation.

claims.statement: In a weak-tunneling description with a sufficiently smooth tip spectrum and matrix element, low-temperature differential conductance can approximate a sample's local density of states. Thermal and instrumental convolution, spatially varying set points and orbital sensitivity can change that relation. A conductance map and an ideal local-density-of-states calculation should not be treated as interchangeable without testing these assumptions.

claims.statement: Taking just $-\operatorname{Im}\Lambda(\mathbf q)/\pi$ is insufficient for a general complex Fourier map. It becomes valid with the additional even-in-momentum response condition. Six independent checks compare full real-space resolvent inversion with the scattering expression on a ten-site, fixed-gap model; displaced defects expose the lost phase. This is a normalization and response check, not a cuprate or FeSe simulation. The selected Wang–Lee manuscript supplies the broader scattering framework and explicitly discusses off-shell and matrix-element limits. Its Eq. (1) includes both Nambu diagonal blocks; the expression here uses an explicitly spin-resolved electron block and a discrete lattice normalization. These local conventions and their checks are not a verbatim reproduction of the full source formula.

claims.statement: A joint-density-of-states construction counts candidate equal-energy connections but omits scattering amplitudes and coherence factors. In an ideal equal-magnitude, real-gap Fermi-surface limit, scalar and magnetic Born amplitudes contain $uu'-vv'$ and $uu'+vv'$. Setting $u=u'=1/\sqrt2$ and $v=\operatorname{sgn}(\Delta)/\sqrt2$ interchanges their zero/nonzero weights when the relative gap sign changes. This conditional example explains sensitivity to the impurity channel; it does not identify a real defect from one bright peak.

claims.statement: Sprau and colleagues' FeSe manuscript reports imaging at 280 mK. The relative-sign analysis uses the real parts at opposite energies, isolates an interband momentum region and places the Fourier origin at a defect. Selected supplementary passages vary the integration area and repeat the analysis on additional impurities. The reported sign inference is conditional on their scattering model and band assignment; it is not an inference from the absolute Fourier intensity alone.

claims.statement: For $N_x$ equally spaced pixels of spacing $a_x$, the periodic-transform length is $L_x=N_xa_x$ and angular-wavevector bin spacing is $2\pi/L_x$; the Nyquist bound is $\pi/a_x$. Using cycles per length removes the $2\pi$ factors. Zero padding interpolates the transform but does not create a larger measured field. A window trades spectral leakage against peak width, so bin spacing alone is not an experimental uncertainty or guaranteed resolving power.

claims.statement: Energy dispersion supports a scattering interpretation only together with band, defect and temperature/field controls. Weak dispersion over a limited window does not by itself prove charge order; Bragg, structural, moire and electronic features can overlap. Conversely, an order and QPI may coexist. The cuprate octet geometry must not be imposed on arbitrary multiband spectra.
